subtitle: Practice noticing who leads disability services decisions, learning from the history self-advocates teach, sharing real power with self-advocates and families, and carrying that spirit into how frontline teams are led.
audience: For program leads, supervisors, managers and senior leaders in disability services and across the agency who shape decisions affecting people with disabilities and want their teams to learn from disability-led leadership.

lessons.title: What disability-led leadership asks of a leader
objectives: Distinguish self-advocates leading a decision from self-advocates being consulted about it.
Describe self-advocacy and self-determination as forms of leadership rather than personal stories.
Identify who is leading one current decision in your area and whose expertise shapes it.
Explain which parts of a decision are fixed and which are open for others to lead.
lessons.teaching:
Disability-led leadership means people with disabilities lead the decisions that shape their own lives and services. The idea grows from self-advocacy, the work of people with disabilities speaking and organizing for themselves and each other, and from families who organized alongside them. Minnesota has a long connection to this work. Partners in Policymaking was created in Minnesota in 1987 as a leadership program for adults with disabilities and parents of young children with developmental disabilities, and the Minnesota Governor's Council on Developmental Disabilities offers it today. Its graduates work in partnership with elected officials to improve how people with disabilities live, work and are educated.

Self-determination puts personal choice at the center. The Council's Partners in Living course pairs self-determination with personal choice, person-centered planning and planning for the future, and it notes that a meaningful life does not look the same for everyone. For a leader, the point is practical. A person who lives with a disability and has learned to navigate services holds expertise that professional training does not supply. Disability may be visible or not, and colleagues may bring this expertise to work without choosing to disclose a disability. Participation and personal disclosure must remain voluntary. Treat it as leadership, not as an inspiring story shared at the start of a meeting and then set aside.

Leading and being consulted are different roles. When people are consulted, staff set the question, write the draft and decide what to do with the comments. When people lead, they help decide what the problem is, what the work should produce and how success will be judged. Many agency processes default to consultation because it is familiar and fits our timelines. Ask yourself where you learned that default and who it leaves out. Then look at one decision in front of you and ask: who is leading here, and whose expertise about disabled lives shapes this decision?

Sharing leadership does not mean handing over decisions that belong to someone else. Laws, funding rules and formal determinations stay with the responsible program area, and legal questions go to legal counsel. Within your authority, look for parts of the process people can genuinely lead: setting an agenda, drafting, presenting or evaluating the result. Check applicable requirements before promising control over any part. Say plainly which parts are open and which are fixed, so nobody is invited to lead a decision that has already been made. The Council's free online Partners courses are a good way to keep learning from this tradition.
lessons.keyPoint: Consultation asks people to react to work that staff have already framed. Disability-led leadership means people with disabilities help frame the question, shape the work and judge the result.
lessons.example: Practice case: Ines, a policy lead in disability services, is revising the plain-language guide that explains a waiver change to the people who use it. Her team usually writes a draft and sends it out for comment. Jonah, who chairs a self-advocacy group that has worked with the division for years, says members want to do more than comment this time. They want to shape what the guide covers. Ines has six weeks and a set of rule changes the guide must explain accurately.
lessons.question: What should Ines do next?
choices: Send the group an early draft instead of a final one, allow a longer comment period, and promise a written answer to every comment.
Invite Jonah to join her drafting team so that a self-advocate's view is present at every step of the work.
Meet with the group to agree what the guide must cover, which rule details are fixed, and which parts members will draft or test.
feedback: An earlier draft and written replies are real improvements. Staff still choose the questions and the content, so members remain reviewers of a guide written about them.

A continuing seat can carry real influence, depending on its authority and support. This offer alone does not answer the group’s request to shape the guide together; ask members which roles they want rather than assuming Jonah represents everyone.
This is the strongest response. Ines is honest about what is fixed, shares the decisions that are open, and lets members lead where their expertise matters most.
lessons.reflection: Where did you learn that consultation is the normal way to involve people? What would change in your work if the people affected helped set the question?
lessons.action: Pick one decision your area will make in the next month. Write two sentences: who frames the question now, and where people with disabilities first have a say. Note one step where they could help set the question instead.

check.question: Which situation shows self-advocates leading a piece of work rather than being consulted about it?
check.correct: They help decide the questions and what the work will produce, from the start.
wrong: They review an early outline, and staff revise the plan in response to each comment.
They hold several seats on a working group that staff chair and set the agenda for.
check.feedback: Consultation, even when done well, asks people to react to work that staff have framed. Leading means helping to set the question, shape the work and judge the result, within the parts that law and funding leave open.

lessons.title: History as a leadership lesson
objectives: Explain why good intentions did not protect people with developmental disabilities from segregation and harm.
Identify present-day warning signs that a well-meant plan may repeat an old pattern.
Apply four history questions to a proposal before it is approved.
Name a pattern in a process, rather than blaming a person, when a plan repeats that history.
lessons.teaching:
Disability history is a practical tool for leaders today. The Council's Partners in Time course follows how people with developmental disabilities lived, learned and worked from ancient times to today. It describes a long record of discrimination, segregation, abuse, ignorance and silence, including times when kind intentions still produced harmful results. It also traces the changes that moved society toward greater inclusion, and it asks learners to notice how history repeats itself.

Good intentions are not the same as good results. The point about kind intentions matters most for leaders, because harm can come from people who mean well. The pattern to watch for is a decision made about people, without them, for reasons that sound caring: safety, efficiency, specialized help or protection. Those reasons can be real. The risk is that they carry the decision without anyone checking, with the people affected, whether it serves them. A plan that separates people by disability deserves a second look, even when the separation is offered as a kindness.

Four history questions help you test a proposal before it is approved. First, does this plan separate people by disability, and who asked for that? Second, who designed it, and did people who would use it take part from the start? Third, what does the plan assume people cannot do, and what evidence supports that assumption? Fourth, if the people affected disagree, can they change it, decline it or choose something else? Write down the answers before the proposal goes forward, and share them with the people who will decide. Resolve important gaps before approval. If a concern involves rights, safety or access, use the appropriate reporting and review process promptly; discussion does not replace required action.

Learning from history is not about blaming the people who came before you or the colleagues around you today. Good intentions do not remove responsibility for correcting harm. The lesson is about systems: habits of deciding for people become routine when nobody asks these questions. When you notice the pattern, name it as a pattern in the process, bring in the people affected, and take questions about eligibility, rights or service decisions to the responsible program area. Partners in Time is free and self-paced, and it is worth taking before your next redesign.
lessons.keyPoint: Some of the harm in disability history came from decisions made for people rather than with them, even for reasons that sounded kind. Test your plans for that pattern before they are approved.
lessons.example: Practice case: Rahul manages a team in an economic assistance program. After complaints about long phone waits, staff design a separate line and appointment process for 'clients who need extra help', meaning older adults and people with disabilities. Staff built the plan in two meetings, and nobody who would use it took part. Launch is set for next month. Rahul's deputy, Corinne, asks whether callers will be routed to the separate line whether they want it or not. The current service remains available during a brief redesign, and Rahul has confirmed that the review can occur without delaying urgent assistance or required deadlines.
lessons.question: What should Rahul do before launch?
choices: Delay launch briefly, bring in people who would use the line, and redesign it as an option callers choose, alongside better support on the main line.
Launch on schedule, since the waits are real, and survey callers after six months to see whether the separate line is working for them.
Drop the separate line and keep one queue for everyone, so that no caller is ever sorted by age or disability, and look again at the waits.
feedback: This is the strongest response in these circumstances. Keep existing access and urgent assistance available while callers help shape an optional route. Confirm that the revised design meets access requirements before launch; a preference survey alone does not establish compliance.
The waits are real and measuring matters. Launching first means people live with a design they had no part in, and a later survey asks them to judge it, not shape it.
Avoiding separation is a sound instinct, but deciding alone repeats the pattern from the other side. Some callers might want a different route if they helped design it.
lessons.reflection: When have you seen a kind reason, such as safety or efficiency, carry a decision that the people affected never shaped? What made it feel settled?
lessons.action: Before your next proposal, process change or redesign goes forward, answer the four history questions from this lesson. Share your answers with the people who will decide, and ask who else should answer them.

check.question: What warning does the history in Partners in Time hold for a leader today?
check.correct: Kind intentions do not prevent harm when people are left out of the decisions.
wrong: Harm happened mainly because earlier leaders did not care about people.
Current rules make the old patterns very unlikely to return in today's services.
check.feedback: The course describes harm that came partly from good intentions. The lesson for leaders is about process: decisions made for people, without them, can repeat old patterns even when everyone involved means well.

lessons.title: Sharing power with self-advocates and families
objectives: Plan a role for self-advocates and family members that includes real decisions, not only comment.
Describe how pay, preparation and support make it possible for people to lead.
Compare three habits for involving people and what each one treats as normal.
Identify which parts of a payment or access question belong with a responsible partner.
lessons.teaching:
Sharing power starts with a role that carries real decisions. The National Frontline Supervisor Competencies, from the University of Minnesota's Institute on Community Integration, include seeking the views of people receiving supports and their families when organizations develop policies and procedures, and even state and federal rules. The Council's Partners in Making Your Case course teaches self-advocates and families how policy is made, how to meet with policymakers, give testimony and organize with others. The self-advocacy tradition prepares people to act on policy, not only to comment on it.

The following meeting patterns are a reflection exercise using terms from the intercultural development continuum. They cannot establish a person’s developmental orientation or substitute for a qualified assessment. A Minimization habit treats everyone the same: one meeting format, one comment period, one set of documents, open to all. It feels fair, and it quietly assumes the professional way of meeting is the normal way. An Acceptance habit notices the difference: long midday meetings, dense documents and unpaid time suit staff, whose job this is, and not people who volunteer, work elsewhere or use supports. An Adaptation habit changes the process itself, with members, and then checks with them whether the change worked.

Three practical supports can make leadership more accessible: compensation, preparation and meaningful decision roles. Seek an authorized way to compensate time and expertise, and confirm funding, eligibility, terms and approval before promising payment or asking people to begin paid work. Second, prepare and support people: share plain-language materials well ahead, offer a briefing before each meeting, and ask what helps each person take part, whether that is a support person, captions, breaks, another format or time to respond in writing. Disability may be visible or not, so ask everyone rather than guessing. Third, share leadership through a self-advocate co-chair, members setting part of the agenda, and members reviewing what their advice changed.

Paying people and meeting access needs often depend on partners in other areas. Whether and how your area can pay people, through a contract, a stipend or another route, is a question for the responsible program area and its finance and contract staff, with legal counsel where needed. Access requests from public participants go through your area's access process, and employee accommodation questions go to Human Resources. A leader's part is to raise these questions early, budget for them and keep members informed. Explain limits early and invite people to choose whether and how to participate. Do not treat willingness to volunteer as evidence that payment barriers are unimportant. Access obligations still apply even when a compensation request cannot be approved.
lessons.keyPoint: Meaningful participation includes influence over the agenda, preparation, access support and a clear account of what advice changed. Seek approved compensation and explain its terms before participation.
lessons.example: Practice case: Mei, a program consultant in the division, staffs an advisory group that reviews service changes with lead agency partners. Members include self-advocates and parents, and none are paid. Meetings run three hours at midday, materials arrive the night before, and staff present most of the time. Attendance has fallen by half. Abdi, a self-advocate and one of the longest-serving members, tells Mei that people feel they are there to approve decisions already made.
lessons.question: What should Mei do first?
choices: Send materials a week early with a plain-language summary, shorten meetings to ninety minutes, and keep the agenda and format as they are.
Ask members to help redesign how the group works, including pay, timing and agenda, and take the payment question to the responsible program area.
Replace most meetings with an online survey after each change, so more self-advocates and parents can respond on their own schedule.
feedback: Earlier materials and shorter meetings help, and members will notice. Staff still decide what is discussed and how, so members remain reviewers of decisions already shaped.
This is the strongest response. Mei changes the process with members rather than for them, and starts on the pay question, which shows their expertise is valued as work.
A survey can reach more people and suits some of them well. It also removes the one place where members shape decisions together, which is the concern Abdi raised.
lessons.reflection: Which of your meeting habits feel normal to you because they suit your job? How might they look to someone who gives up unpaid time to take part?
lessons.action: Look at one group, meeting or review your area runs with people outside the agency. Write down who sets the agenda, who is paid and how access needs are asked about. Choose one change to raise with the group.

check.question: Which change does the most to shift power to self-advocates in an advisory group?
check.correct: Members help set the agenda and can see what their advice changed.
wrong: Members receive plain-language materials a week before every meeting.
More self-advocate seats are added so members outnumber staff at meetings.
check.feedback: Earlier materials and more seats help people take part, but staff still frame the work. Power shifts when members help decide what is discussed and can see what their advice changed.

lessons.title: Leading frontline teams in the same spirit
objectives: Explain how the National Frontline Supervisor Competencies connect frontline supervision to self-advocacy and choice.
Identify ways a leader can involve direct support professionals in decisions about their work.
Distinguish what a state leader can suggest to a provider from what the provider decides.
Plan one change in your role that brings people receiving services or frontline staff into a decision.
lessons.teaching:
Disability-led leadership has to reach the people who provide support every day. Direct support professionals help people with disabilities live the lives they choose, and their supervisors shape how that support happens. The National Frontline Supervisor Competencies, developed at the University of Minnesota's Research and Training Center on Community Living, describe 11 areas of skill for supervisors of direct support professionals in intellectual and developmental disability services. Three areas speak directly to this course: advocacy and public relations; leadership, professionalism and self-development; and cultural awareness and responsiveness.

The National Frontline Supervisor Competencies treat choice and self-advocacy as part of the supervisor's job. They describe person-centered support that gives people as much choice and control as possible, promoting self-advocacy when someone meets barriers, and teaching advocacy skills to people receiving services, families and staff. The source emphasizes individuals and families in decisions about their lives. In practice, center the person receiving support, ask whom they want involved, and verify any representative’s authority. Family involvement alone does not establish authority to decide for an adult. They also ask supervisors to seek direct support professionals' ideas, let them make decisions and run meetings that build trust and shared ownership. Keep the limits in mind: the set dates from 2013, was written for provider organizations in intellectual and developmental disability services, and builds on a 2007 study in which direct support staff, supervisors and managers rated how important each skill was, plus expert review. It shows which skills the field values, not that training on them improves outcomes.

You can bring disability-led values into any frontline work you lead or shape. First, ask before you decide: when a change affects how support is given, ask frontline staff and people receiving services what they see, and let their answers change the plan. Second, share decisions with the team, not only tasks, so the people closest to the work help set how it is done. Third, make self-advocacy part of ordinary practice by checking that people know how to raise a concern and who will listen. In state work, the same moves apply when you design training expectations, review provider practice or plan a workforce effort.

Your role has limits when the work belongs to a provider or another area. Supervisors at provider organizations work within their employer's policies, licensing requirements and any labor agreement, and a training discussion does not authorize state staff to direct a provider’s personnel decisions. Applicable oversight, reporting and enforcement duties still follow their established processes. Hiring, discipline and pay questions for agency staff belong with Human Resources and labor relations. Use the competency set as a source of ideas, not as a checklist for rating anyone. The Institute on Community Integration offers it as a free download, and it can open a useful conversation with providers and self-advocates about good frontline leadership.
lessons.keyPoint: Frontline leadership carries disability-led values into daily support: people choose, the staff closest to the work help decide, and self-advocacy is part of ordinary practice.
lessons.example: Practice case: Kofi works in provider relations for the division and is helping a provider plan a development day for its frontline supervisors. The draft agenda, written by the provider's managers, covers documentation and compliance. Nobody who receives services or works in direct support helped plan it. Lena, the provider's training lead and a self-advocate who has worked there for years, asks Kofi whether the state would support another approach. The agenda is the provider's to set.
lessons.question: What should Kofi suggest?
choices: Recommend adding a session on person-centered practice to the current agenda, led by the provider's managers, and share the competency set.
Tell Lena that the agenda belongs to the provider's managers, and offer to share state training materials if the managers ask for them.
Suggest the provider plan the day with Lena, two direct support staff and people receiving services, using the competency set as a starting point.
feedback: Adding the topic is a step, and the competency set is useful. The same managers would still plan alone, so the day would teach person-centered practice without practicing it.
Respecting the provider's authority is right, since the agenda is theirs. Stepping back entirely leaves Lena's question unanswered and misses a chance to support a better process.
This is the strongest response. Kofi respects that the provider decides, and offers a way of planning that brings people receiving services and frontline staff to the table.
lessons.reflection: When did someone closest to the work last change a decision you made? What made it possible for them to speak up, and what might have stopped them?
lessons.action: Choose one decision your area will make soon. Write down who is leading it, answer the four history questions, and name one point where a self-advocate, family member or frontline worker could help shape it. Share your note with whoever owns the decision.

check.question: A team is changing how a routine support task is done. Which step best carries disability-led values into that change?
check.correct: Ask the staff and the people they support what they see, and let their answers change the plan.
wrong: Explain the change clearly at a team meeting and give everyone time to ask questions first.
Train staff in person-centered practice before the change so they can carry it out well.
check.feedback: Explaining and training are useful, but staff still receive a plan made without them. Disability-led values mean the people closest to the work help shape it, and their answers can change it.

cards.back: People with disabilities speaking and acting for themselves and for each other, from everyday choices to organizing for changes in policy and services.

Compensation for participation through an authorized route, with approval and clear terms before paid work begins. Do not promise a stipend or contract until the responsible staff confirm it is available.
People with disabilities leading decisions about their lives, their services and the policies that affect them, as leaders rather than as people consulted.
Consulted people react to questions and drafts that staff have framed. People who lead help set the question, shape the work and judge whether it worked.
A worker who supports a person with a disability in daily life, at home, at work or in the community, in the way that person chooses.

aid.heading: Before a decision is framed
items: Ask who is leading this decision and whose expertise about disabled lives shapes it.
Does the plan separate people by disability, and who asked for that?
Who designed it, and did people who would use it take part from the start?
What does the plan assume people cannot do, and what evidence supports that?
If the people affected disagree, can they change it, decline it or choose something else?

aid.heading: When you run a group or review with people outside the agency
items: Confirm an authorized payment route, approval and terms before promising compensation or starting paid work.
Send plain-language materials well ahead and offer a briefing before meetings.
Ask everyone what helps them take part instead of guessing.
Share the agenda and the chair with members.
Show members what their advice changed, and what it did not.

aid.heading: What needs a partner
items: Payment routes and contracts go to the responsible program area and its finance staff.
Access requests from public participants go through your area's access process.
Employee accommodation questions go to Human Resources.
Say which parts are fixed by law or funding and which are open; take legal questions to legal counsel.
Respect provider personnel authority while following applicable oversight and reporting duties.
